title: Checkpoint: Buddhism and Sikhism
objective: After this level you can explain the core teachings, practices and branches of Buddhism and Sikhism and why each began.
summary: Two faiths of the Indian family: the Buddha's path from suffering to nirvana, and Guru Nanak's one God and equality, carried on in the Guru Granth Sahib and the Khalsa.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: two faiths born in India, in their own words.
cards.body: One began with a prince who left home, the other with a man who came back from a river. Line up the key moments, then see what you can now explain.

cards.headline: Key moments in Buddhism and Sikhism

events.label: The Buddha dies, as scholars date it
Guru Gobind Singh founds the Khalsa

items.label: Buddhism
points: Began with the Buddha's awakening at Bodh Gaya
Aims at nirvana, the end of suffering and rebirth
Lives in a sangha of monastics and laypeople

items.label: Sikhism
points: Began with Guru Nanak's message in Punjab
Its Guru today is the Guru Granth Sahib
Puts equality into practice in the langar and the Khalsa

cards.headline: Two communities today
cards.body: In 2020 about 4 percent of the world's people were Buddhist. Sikhs number about 25 million, most of them in India's Punjab state. Both faiths live as communities as much as teachings: a sangha of monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen, and a Panth gathered around the Guru Granth Sahib.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 complete
learned: Why the Buddha taught that suffering has a cause and can end, and how the middle way leads there.
What historians can confirm about the Buddha, and how Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana differ.
How monks, nuns and laypeople support each other, from the alms round to Vesak.
Why Guru Nanak's one God and equality led to the langar, the Granth as Guru and the Khalsa.

questions.prompt: Put these Sikh milestones in order: the Adi Granth compiled, the Khalsa founded, the scripture becomes Guru.

options.label: Adi Granth, then Khalsa, then scripture as Guru
Khalsa, then Adi Granth, then scripture as Guru
options.rationale: The Adi Granth (1604) came before the Khalsa (1699).

options.label: Scripture as Guru, then Adi Granth, then Khalsa
options.rationale: The scripture became Guru last, in 1708.

options.label: Adi Granth, then scripture as Guru, then Khalsa

questions.prompt: A Buddhist friend says, "If I stop grasping, suffering loosens its hold." Which teaching is she drawing on?

options.label: The Four Noble Truths: craving causes suffering
The Five Ks: articles of faith
options.rationale: Those are Sikh articles of faith.

options.label: The refuge formula of the Three Jewels
options.rationale: Refuge makes you a Buddhist; it doesn't explain suffering.

options.label: The langar: equality at the meal
options.rationale: That is a Sikh practice of equality.

questions.explanation: The second truth names craving as the cause of suffering, and the third says removing it brings suffering to an end.

questions.prompt: Why do the arhat of Theravada and the bodhisattva of Mahayana represent different ideals?

options.label: The arhat worships many gods; the bodhisattva one
options.rationale: The difference is about whose awakening comes first.

options.label: One seeks awakening by own effort; one delays it to help all
The arhat lives in Tibet; the bodhisattva in Sri Lanka
The arhat is a layperson; the bodhisattva must be a monk
options.rationale: Mahayana teaches anyone can become a bodhisattva.

questions.explanation: The arhat reaches enlightenment through their own effort; the bodhisattva delays nirvana to help all beings.

questions.prompt: About how many Sikhs are there in the world?

options.label: About 2.5 million
About 25 million
About 250 million
About 2.5 billion

questions.explanation: Sikhs number about 25 million, most in India's Punjab state.

questions.prompt: An alms bowl and a langar meal both involve food. What does each show?

options.label: Alms: a tax to the king; langar: food sold to pilgrims
options.rationale: Both are free gifts, not taxes or sales.

options.label: Both are meals only for monks and nuns
Both mark the start of a new year
Alms: monks and laypeople sustain each other; langar: all eat as equals

questions.explanation: Alms bind monastics and laypeople through food, blessing and merit; the langar seats everyone in one line as equals.
